name: Croatian klapa Dalmatian close-harmony
lineage: Croatian klapa Dalmatian close-harmony multipart-singing tradition of the Adriatic coastal region (Split, Šibenik, Zadar, Dubrovnik and the Adriatic islands). The classical klapa configuration is a male a-cappella quartet or quintet: lead tenor (prvi tenor), second tenor (drugi tenor), baritone (bariton), and bass (bas), with the optional addition of a second bass voice for fuller texture. Vocal architecture features close-harmony chordal-block writing (almost always homophonic, with all voices moving together rhythmically), characteristic Mediterranean modal-tonal ambiguity (major-mode tonic with frequent flattened-seventh and minor-mode plagal cadences), and the canonical klapa "Dalmatian" intonation with slightly stretched intervals producing a bright, resonant ensemble sound when sung in stone-walled outdoor narrow-street alleys (the canonical performance acoustic). Repertoire spans the dramatic Mediterranean-coastal love-and-loss ballad cycles, the religious-procession-and-feast-day repertoire, sea-and-fishing lament cycles, and the contemporary klapa-festival-composed repertoire of newer pieces in the traditional style. Klapa Cambi, Klapa Šufit, and Klapa Sebenico among the canonical twentieth-century ensembles. The annual Omiš Festival of Dalmatian Klapa (founded 1967) constitutes the principal performance-and-competition venue. Distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore by Croatian klapa's close-harmony tonal-chord-block (vs Sardinian drone-and-overtone) architecture; distinguished from Corsican paghjella by Croatian's four-or-five-voice quartet-with-bass (vs Corsican's three-voice male-trio) configuration; distinguished from Albanian iso-polyphony by Croatian's tonal-chord-block (vs Albanian iso-drone) foundation.
